speaker: martinpastucha
text: and members of the City Council. As you'll see in the presentation, this is a necessary step for the project should negotiations with property owners not prove successful and to avoid a potential delay or even cancellation of the project due to funding loss. speaker: Other
text: Great, thank you. So this is for, as Martin said earlier, for Rainier Avenue South corridor improvements, phase four. It's an extension of the improvements that were done on phase three, which is from, I believe, 167 to South 3rd, or North 3rd Place. So the improvements will begin at South 3rd Street and continue just beyond the airport to North 3rd Place. And right now we have, we're in design and we're just about at 100%. So the real critical path here now is right of way and continuing the negotiations with the property owners along the corridor. Some of the project goals for Rainier Avenue is to improve transit mobility, pedestrian accessibility, and safety. It'll benefit overall traffic flow through access management, traffic signal updates, and coordination. We'll be putting in a median along the road, which will help with access management. We'll improve the pedestrian environment and safety, and then improving the intersections at South 3rd Street and South 2nd Street. And this is in preparation of converting South 2nd and South 3rd to two-way traffic operations. It will also construct a segment of the Lake Washington Loop Trail from Airport Way to Northwest 3rd Place. And then it will put in two pedestrian-activated traffic signals, hawk signals, at Southwest Victoria and Northwest 3rd Place. And then there'll be sidewalk widening. We'll be widening the sidewalks to eight feet in most places. And then there'll also be planter strips, streetscaping, and making it overall a more vibrant corridor. So the project budget, we have a lot of funding sources and a lot of grants that are coming in for this project. There was a $2.6 million grant for preliminary engineering, a $3 million grant for right-of-way. We've received $4.5 million for construction, and then another $4.793 for construction. And more recently, a $2 million Regional Mobility Grant also for construction. The last bit is a $5 million TIB grant that we have requested, and we're hoping to hear back later this month with some good news. And then as far as the schedule goes, we are in, we've been at 90% design now for a little bit of time, because the driving factor and the critical path has been the right-of-way acquisition. With that being said, our 100% design should be complete any moment. And then once the 100% design is completed, we'll submit to WSDOT for approval. And at the same time that we submit to WSDOT for approval for the design, we're hope, well, with the passing of the ordinance for the condemnation, we're hoping that we'll be able to also submit for our certification. Not hoping, we need to submit for our certification in order to maintain our grant deadlines for obligation. And the plan is then to advertise in the summer of 2022, so just this next year, and then construction beginning in fall of 2022. And we're anticipating about a two-year construction, or two years for construction. And again, the right-of-way acquisition is the critical path for meeting the funding obligations and beginning construction next summer. So the parcels that are impacted. So there are about 36 or 35 parcels along Rainier that will be impacted by this project. And of those 35 parcels, we're dealing with about 28 different property owners. Some property owners do own more than one parcel. And then, so what we're taking are, so the easements and acquisitions are only strip takes, which allow for the city to meet our current street design standards. And I've kind of included on the side over here what the easements or strip takes look like. So here is a piece that we'll actually be taking, a piece of right-of-way, and then this'll be an easement, and then a temporary construction easement back here. So we're not taking full parcels. It's just strips and small takes in order to accommodate utility easements, slope easements, and then to be able to construct the improvements. So the city has been negotiating to acquire portions of properties for nearly a year. We've obtained five signed agreements and four verbal agreements to enter into acquisition documents. So we're making progress with negotiating with the property owners. So a little bit about the condemnation process itself. In order to meet the timeframes outlined in our grants, the city needs to acquire necessary property rights by March of 2022. If we don't meet the deadlines, the city is at risk of losing millions of dollars in grants for this project. The proposed ordinance authorizes initiation of condemnation proceedings to acquire the property rights needed for the project, which is a prerequisite for the city filing a condemnation lawsuit. It will be necessary to initiate condemnation proceedings in case continued negotiations with property owners are unsuccessful. And the main thing to reiterate here is that we are continuing to negotiate with the property owners. This doesn't in any way replace negotiating with them at this time. It is just in case we are unable to reach agreements with these property owners in order to be able to build the project. So the staff recommendation, the city will continue to negotiate with property owners in order to reach an agreement, but the initiation of condemnation is necessary to acquire the property rights as required by the grant funding for the project. And so we recommend to adopt the proposed ordinance authorizing the initiation of condemnation proceedings for a portion of certain properties on Rainier Avenue South and Rainier Avenue North between South 3rd Street and Northwest 3rd Place. And now is a good time for questions and- Okay.

text: And also, Michelle, just to add, some of these are various takes of different types. As she said, there's a permanent easement that we take.
